lessons.title: Share, co-author, comments and notes
learn: Share a link with view or edit rights
lessons.mac:
• Share button: top-right of the window (save to OneDrive first)
• New comment: ⌘ + ⇧ + M · post: ⌘ + Return
• Review > Notes > New Note
• Right-click a cell (Control-click) for comment and note options

steps.say: This is the team's expense claims sheet after review. One claim had a question about a hotel bill; it was asked, answered and resolved inside the file, and the claim is now approved. Nobody emailed a copy back and forth.

You will learn to share a link with view or edit rights, to work on the same file at the same time as colleagues, and to use comments and notes properly. Practice sheet S15-01, in a file saved on OneDrive.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Share a link: can view or can edit
2. Co-authoring: several people, one file
3. Comments (conversations) vs Notes (sticky labels)

Practice: sheet S15-01 · file must be on OneDrive or SharePoint

steps.say: Two ideas to keep straight. A comment is a conversation: people reply, mention each other and resolve it when done. A note is a simple sticky label on a cell, with no replies.

acts.t:
Comment vs Note

Comment: threaded conversation · @mention sends an email · Resolve when done
Note: a yellow sticky label · no replies · good for permanent explanations

Mac shortcut for a new comment: ⌘ + Shift + M

steps.say: Start with sharing. Click the Share button at the top right. Excel offers to send a link or copy one. The setting under the link decides whether people can edit or only view.
For a finance report going to the whole team, choose Can view. For colleagues who fill in their own rows, choose Can edit. Close the box for now with Escape.
When colleagues open the same link, you see their initials at the top and a coloured box on the cell they are in. Everyone's changes save automatically, so there is only ever one version.

acts.t:
Co-authoring

• Same file, same time: initials at the top, coloured cell borders
• AutoSave on (OneDrive / SharePoint)
• No more 'Claims_final_v3_Rahul.xlsx'
• Mac app: AutoSave toggle at the top-left of the window

steps.say: Now a comment. Karan's hotel claim in F5 is eighteen thousand six hundred rupees. Select F5, and on the Review tab click New Comment.
Type: hotel bill for this claim is missing, please attach it before approval. Press Command Return to post. In real use, type an at sign and a colleague's name to tag them, and they get an email.

acts.h: Type Hotel bill for this claim is missing. Please attach it before approval.

steps.say: Karan replies in the same thread. Click Reply, type: uploaded to the claims folder today, and post it. The whole conversation stays attached to the cell.

acts.h: Type Uploaded to the claims folder today.

steps.say: A common mistake is to delete comments once they are sorted. That throws away the record. Instead, open More thread actions and choose Resolve thread. It is hidden but can be reopened.
Now approve the claim. Click G5, type Approved and press Return.
For a permanent explanation, use a note. Select F9, the eight hundred and seventy rupee client gift. On the Review tab click Notes, then New Note, type the reason, and press Escape.

acts.h: Type Diwali sweets box for client visit, bill attached.

steps.say: Pro tip: click Show Comments on the Review tab to see every thread in one pane, including resolved ones. It is the quickest way to check what is still open before month-end.
On a Mac, the Share button is at the top right of the Excel window, and the file must be on OneDrive or SharePoint. New Comment is Command Shift M. Notes are under Review, Notes, just like here.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Share button: top-right of the window (save to OneDrive first)
• New comment: ⌘ + ⇧ + M · post: ⌘ + Return
• Review > Notes > New Note
• Right-click a cell (Control-click) for comment and note options

steps.say: To recap: share a link and choose view or edit. Use comments for conversations and resolve them when done. Use notes for permanent explanations.

acts.t:
Recap

• Share > link > Can view / Can edit
• Comments: @mention, reply, Resolve
• Notes: sticky explanations, no replies

steps.say: Your challenge: add a comment on F12 asking whether the travel claim needs a manager's approval, reply to it yourself, and resolve it. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Comment on F12, reply, then Resolve the thread.
Add a note on any 'Local conveyance' claim.

Compare: sheet S15-01 Done

lessons.title: Version history and Sheet View
lessons.mac:
• Version history: File > Browse Version History (or click the file name in the title bar)
• Sheet View: View tab > New / Keep / Exit (Microsoft 365, file on OneDrive or SharePoint)
• Filter shortcut: ⌘ + ⇧ + F

steps.say: This is what you will see in your own Sheet View: only the South region, six rows. At the same moment, your colleagues still see all twenty-four rows. And if someone breaks the file, version history brings back last week's copy.
You will learn to open version history and restore an older copy, and to filter or sort a shared file in a Sheet View without disturbing anyone. Practice sheet S15-02, saved on OneDrive.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Version history: view and restore old copies
2. Sheet View: your own filter and sort in a shared file
3. Exit and keep views

Practice: sheet S15-02 · file on OneDrive

steps.say: OneDrive keeps a copy of your file every time it saves. Version history lists those copies by date and person. Sheet View solves another problem: in a shared file, a normal filter hides rows for everyone.

acts.t:
Two safety nets

Version history: every saved version, by date and author → open or restore
Sheet View: a private view of a shared sheet → filter and sort only for you

Both need the file on OneDrive or SharePoint.

steps.say: Go to the File tab and click Info, then Version History. A list of saved versions opens, newest first, each with a date, time and the person who saved it.

Click any older version to open it read-only. If it is the one you want, click Restore, and it becomes the current version. The version you replaced is kept in the list too, so restoring is never final.

acts.t:
Restore last week's file

1. File > Info > Version History
2. Click a version (opens read-only)
3. Restore → it becomes the current version

Need just one number? Copy it from the old version instead of restoring.

steps.say: Close version history and go back to the sheet.
Now the common mistake. Turn on the normal filter with Command Shift F. If you filter Region to South now, the other regions disappear for every colleague who has the file open.
Switch the filter off again with the same shortcut. Instead, on the View tab, click New in the Sheet View group. The row and column headings turn dark, which tells you that you are in your own view.
Now filter freely. Turn on the filter, open the arrow on Region, untick Select All, tick South and click OK. Only the six South rows remain, but only for you.
Sort as well. Select D1 and choose Sort Descending on the Data tab. The South reps are now ranked by sales, and still nobody else is affected.
To save this view, click Keep on the View tab; it is named Temporary View, and you can rename it in Options. To go back to what everyone sees, click Exit.
Back in the Default view, all twenty-four rows are there in their original order. Your South view is one click away in the Sheet View list.

On a Mac, Version History is under File, Browse Version History, or the file name at the top of the window. Sheet View is on the View tab of Excel for Mac with Microsoft 365, for files on OneDrive or SharePoint.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Version history: File > Browse Version History (or click the file name in the title bar)
• Sheet View: View tab > New / Keep / Exit (Microsoft 365, file on OneDrive or SharePoint)
• Filter shortcut: ⌘ + ⇧ + F

steps.say: To recap: version history keeps every save and lets you restore one. In a shared file, filter and sort inside a Sheet View. Exit returns you to what everyone sees.

acts.t:
Recap

• File > Info > Version History > Restore
• View > New Sheet View before filtering a shared file
• Keep to save it, Exit to leave

steps.say: Your challenge: create a Sheet View that shows only May twenty-six, sorted by sales from highest to lowest, keep it, and rename it May Ranking. Compare your South view with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

New Sheet View → filter Month = May-26 → sort Sales Z→A → Keep → rename 'May Ranking'.

South-only view for comparison: sheet S15-02 Done

lessons.title: Protect cells, sheets and workbooks
learn: Unlock input cells, lock the rest
lessons.mac:
• ⌘ + 1 > Protection: Locked / Hidden
• Review > Protect Sheet, Protect Workbook
• File > Passwords… for a password to open or modify
• Excel for the web: Review > Manage Protection

steps.say: This budget request form goes to every department. People can type in the yellow cells, but the GST and total formulas are locked and hidden, and nobody can delete or rename the sheet. That stops accidental damage.
You will learn to unlock input cells, lock and hide formulas, protect the sheet, and protect the workbook structure. Practice sheet S15-03. This is recorded in Excel desktop; the Mac menus match.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Unlock input cells (Format Cells > Protection)
2. Hide formulas
3. Protect Sheet and Protect Workbook

Practice: sheet S15-03 · Mac: Review tab, ⌘ + 1

steps.say: Every cell starts out Locked, but Locked does nothing until you protect the sheet. So the order is: first unlock the cells people should type in, then protect the sheet.

acts.t:
How protection works

Every cell is Locked by default
Locked only matters once the sheet is protected

1. Unlock input cells
2. (Optional) tick Hidden on formula cells
3. Review > Protect Sheet

steps.say: First, the common mistake. On the Review tab, click Protect Sheet and click OK straight away. Now try to correct a quantity in B8. Excel refuses, because every cell, including the inputs, is still locked.
Click Unprotect Sheet on the Review tab. Now select the input cells: B3 to B4, and A7 to C11, together.
Press Command 1 to open Format Cells. Go to the Protection tab, untick Locked, and click OK.
Next, the formulas. Select D7 to F12, open Format Cells again, and on the Protection tab tick Hidden. Hidden formulas won't show in the formula bar once the sheet is protected.
Now click Protect Sheet. You can type a password here, but if you forget it, nobody can recover it, so store it safely. We'll leave it blank for practice and click OK.

Test it. The brochure quote has come down to eight thousand rupees, so type eight thousand in C9. It works, and the total in F12 drops to three lakh twenty-five thousand four hundred and forty-four rupees.
Click F12. The formula bar is empty, because the formula is hidden. Try typing over it, and Excel shows the protected sheet message. Click OK.

Sheet protection doesn't stop someone deleting or renaming the sheet. For that, click Protect Workbook on the Review tab, keep Structure ticked, and click OK. Sheets can no longer be added, deleted, moved or renamed.

Pro tip: sheet protection is about preventing mistakes, not security. Anyone determined can get around it. To keep a file confidential, set a password to open it, or share it only with the right people on OneDrive.

acts.t:
Pro tip

Protect Sheet / Workbook = guard rails against accidents
Real security = password to open (Mac: File > Passwords…) or OneDrive sharing permissions
Keep passwords in a password manager: Excel can't recover them.

steps.say: On a Mac, Format Cells is Command 1, with the same Protection tab. Protect Sheet and Protect Workbook are on the Review tab. A password to open the file is under File, Passwords.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• ⌘ + 1 > Protection: Locked / Hidden
• Review > Protect Sheet, Protect Workbook
• File > Passwords… for a password to open or modify
• Excel for the web: Review > Manage Protection

steps.say: To recap: unlock inputs first, hide formulas if you like, then protect the sheet. Protect the workbook to lock the sheet structure. Protection prevents accidents; it isn't encryption.

acts.t:
Recap

• Unlock inputs → Protect Sheet
• Hidden = formula not shown in the formula bar
• Protect Workbook = no adding, deleting or renaming sheets

steps.say: Your challenge: unprotect the sheet and protect it again so that users can still widen columns, but nothing else changes. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Unprotect, then Protect Sheet again so users may widen columns.
Which box do you tick?

Answer: sheet S15-03 Done, cell H3

lessons.title: Printing and PDF
learn: Print area, print titles, fit to one page wide
lessons.mac:
• Page Layout tab: Print Area, Print Titles, Breaks, Orientation, Size
• File > Page Setup: Page, Margins, Header/Footer, Sheet tabs
• PDF: File > Save As > File Format: PDF
  or ⌘ + P > PDF > Save as PDF

steps.say: Here is a sixty-row sales register set up for printing: landscape on A4, one page wide, headings repeated on every page, a page number in the footer, and a page break where we chose. It prints, or saves as a PDF, exactly like this.

You will learn to set a print area, repeat the heading row, fit all columns on one page wide, add headers and footers, insert a page break and create a PDF. Practice sheet S15-04, recorded in Excel desktop.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Print Area and Print Titles
2. Landscape, A4, fit to 1 page wide
3. Header, footer, page breaks
4. Save as PDF

Practice: sheet S15-04 · Mac: Page Layout tab, File > Page Setup

steps.say: Most print problems come from three settings. Print Area decides what prints. Print Titles repeat the header row on every page. Fit to one page wide stops the last columns from spilling onto extra pages.

acts.t:
Three settings that fix most printouts

Print Area: only this range prints
Print Titles: rows to repeat at top ($1:$1)
Scaling: Fit to 1 page wide, tall = automatic (blank)

steps.say: Go to sheet S15-04 and select A1 to I62, the register and its total row. On the Page Layout tab, click Print Area, Set Print Area.
Click Print Titles. In Rows to repeat at top, type dollar one colon dollar one. Every printed page will now start with the column headings.

acts.h: Set Rows to repeat at top to $1:$1

steps.say: Switch to the Page tab. Choose Landscape, paper size A4. Under Scaling, choose Fit to one page wide, and clear the tall box so Excel uses as many pages as it needs.
A common mistake is Fit sheet on one page. Sixty rows squeezed onto one sheet of paper become too small to read. One page wide, with the length left blank, is almost always what you want.
On the Header and Footer tab, pick the sheet name for the header and Page 1 of question mark for the footer. Click OK.
The register should break after the first thirty invoices. Select A31, then on the Page Layout tab choose Breaks, Insert Page Break.
On the View tab, click Page Break Preview. Blue lines show each page, with Page 1 and Page 2 written across them. You can drag a blue line to move a break.
Switch back to Normal view. Now the PDF. Go to File, Export, Create PDF slash XPS. Name it S15-04 Sales Register and click Publish.

acts.h: Set File name to S15-04 Sales Register

steps.say: Pro tip: before printing anything long, check the page count in the print preview. If it says twelve pages when you expected two, a stray cell far to the right has probably stretched the printed range.

acts.t:
Pro tip

Check the page count in Print preview (Mac: ⌘ + P).
Too many pages? Look for stray content far right or far down (⌘ + End jumps to the last used cell).

steps.say: On a Mac, Print Area, Print Titles and Breaks are on the Page Layout tab. The full dialog is File, Page Setup. For a PDF, choose File, Save As, and set File Format to PDF, or press Command P and choose Save as PDF.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Page Layout tab: Print Area, Print Titles, Breaks, Orientation, Size
• File > Page Setup: Page, Margins, Header/Footer, Sheet tabs
• PDF: File > Save As > File Format: PDF
  or ⌘ + P > PDF > Save as PDF

steps.say: To recap: set the print area, repeat the heading row, and fit to one page wide. Add a page number footer and check page breaks. Save as PDF to share.

acts.t:
Recap

• Print Area + Print Titles ($1:$1)
• Landscape, A4, 1 page wide
• Footer 'Page 1 of ?', Page Break Preview, Save as PDF

steps.say: Your challenge: add your company name to the right side of the footer, and print gridlines. Compare your page setup with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Custom Footer: company name on the right.
Sheet tab: tick Gridlines.

Compare: sheet S15-04 Done (Page Break Preview)

lessons.title: Linked data types: stocks and geography
learn: Population and capital from a city name
lessons.mac:
• Data tab > Data Types: Stocks, Geography
• Same =A2.Price formulas
• Data > Refresh All
• Microsoft 365 subscription, signed in, online
• Ambiguous name? A ? icon appears: click it and pick the right one

steps.say: Type a few NSE codes and state names, and Excel can fetch live share prices, company names, state capitals and population for you. No copying from websites, and a refresh brings the latest numbers.

acts.t:
Finished result

• A2:A7 NSE codes turned into Stocks: Company, Price, Change (%) beside them
• G2:G7 states turned into Geography: Capital, Population
• Data > Refresh All updates prices
• Sheet S15-05 Done lists the expected capitals

steps.say: You will learn to convert text into the Stocks and Geography data types, to pull fields with a formula, and to refresh. Practice sheet S15-05. You need Microsoft 365 and an internet connection.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Data > Stocks and Data > Geography
2. Fields with the dot: =A2.Price
3. The #FIELD! error and Refresh

Practice: sheet S15-05 · needs Microsoft 365 + internet

steps.say: A linked data type turns a cell into a record with many fields. You read a field by typing the cell, a dot, and the field name. Field names with spaces or symbols go inside square brackets.

acts.t:
Dot syntax

=A2.Price
=A2.Name
=A2.[Change (%)]   ← brackets for spaces/symbols
=G2.Capital
=G2.Population

XNSE: in front of a code picks the National Stock Exchange

steps.say: Select A2 to A7, the NSE codes. On the Data tab, click Stocks. Each code gets a small building icon, which means it is now linked.
In B2, type equals A2 dot Name and press Return. Fill it down to B7 with Command D.

acts.h: Select B2:B7 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In C2, type equals A2 dot Price, and in D2, equals A2 dot, open square bracket, Change percent, close bracket. Fill both down.

acts.h: Select C2:C7 and fill down with ⌘ + D
Select D2:D7 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here is the common mistake. In E2, type equals A2 dot Capital. A company has no capital field, so Excel shows the FIELD error. Press Delete to clear it. Only use fields that exist for that data type.
Now the states. Select G2 to G7 and click Geography on the Data tab. Each name gets a small map icon.
In H2, type equals G2 dot Capital, and in I2, equals G2 dot Population. Fill both down. Maharashtra gives Mumbai, Rajasthan gives Jaipur, Uttar Pradesh gives Lucknow.

acts.h: Select H2:H7 and fill down with ⌘ + D
Select I2:I7 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: There is a mouse route too. Select G2 to G7 and click the Insert Data button that appears beside the cells. Pick Area, and Excel adds the column for you.
Prices don't update on their own. On the Data tab, click Refresh All to fetch the latest numbers. Stock prices can be delayed by some minutes, so don't use them for trading decisions.
On a Mac, Stocks and Geography are in the Data Types group on the Data tab, the same dot formulas work, and refresh is Data, Refresh All. You need Microsoft 365 and to be signed in.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Data tab > Data Types: Stocks, Geography
• Same =A2.Price formulas
• Data > Refresh All
• Microsoft 365 subscription, signed in, online
• Ambiguous name? A ? icon appears: click it and pick the right one

steps.say: To recap: convert text with Data, Stocks or Geography. Pull fields with the dot, using brackets for long names. FIELD errors mean the field doesn't exist for that type.

acts.t:
Recap

• Data > Stocks / Geography
• =A2.Price, =A2.[Change (%)]
• #FIELD! = wrong field · Refresh All for new data

steps.say: Your challenge: add each company's fifty-two week high in E, and each state's largest city in J. The formulas are on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

E2: 52-week high for each stock
J2: largest city for each state
(Hint: type the dot and pick from the list)

Answer: sheet S15-05 Done, cell K4

lessons.title: Templates and accessibility
lessons.mac:
• Review > Check Accessibility
• Alt text: Control-click picture > Edit Alt Text
• File > Save as Template… (.xltx)
• File > New from Template… (⌘ + ⇧ + P)

steps.say: This GST tax invoice is saved as a template. Every new invoice starts from a clean copy, so the master is never overwritten. It also passes the Accessibility Checker, so people using screen readers can follow it.

You will learn to run the Accessibility Checker and fix three common issues: missing alt text, merged cells and faint text. Then you will save the file as your own template. Practice sheet S15-06, recorded in Excel desktop.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Review > Check Accessibility
2. Fix alt text, merged cells, low-contrast text
3. Save as a template (.xltx) and reuse it

Practice: sheet S15-06

steps.say: The checker sorts problems into errors, which make content impossible to read with a screen reader, and warnings, which make it harder. Each item has a recommended fix.

acts.t:
Accessibility Checker

Errors: missing alt text on pictures, charts, shapes
Warnings: merged cells, hard-to-read text contrast, default sheet names

Template: .xltx file. Opening it creates a new untitled copy.

steps.say: Go to sheet S15-06. On the Review tab, click Check Accessibility. The pane lists missing alternative text for Picture 1, merged cells in A1 to F1, and hard-to-read text in A30.
Click Picture 1 in the pane to select the logo. On the Picture Format tab, click Alt Text, and type: Shree Ganesh Traders logo. A screen reader will now read that out.
Next, the title. Merged cells confuse screen readers and break sorting and copying. Select A1 to F1 and click Merge and Center on the Home tab to unmerge it.
The title jumps to the left. To centre it without merging, press Command 1, go to the Alignment tab, set Horizontal to Center Across Selection, and click OK. It looks the same, without the merge.
Last, the thank-you line in A30 is pale grey on white, which many people can't read. Select A30, open Font Color on the Home tab and choose Automatic.

Now the template. The common mistake is to keep one invoice file, overwrite it every time, and lose last month's invoice. Press F12 for Save As, set the type to Excel Template, name it GST Invoice Template, and click Save.

acts.h: Set Save as type to Excel Template (*.xltx)
Set File name to GST Invoice Template

steps.say: From now on, choose File, New, and open the Personal tab. Click GST Invoice Template, and Excel opens an untitled copy. You fill it in and save it as a normal workbook, and the template stays clean.

acts.t:
Use your template

Windows: File > New > Personal > GST Invoice Template
Mac: File > New from Template… > My Templates

Each opens an untitled copy; the .xltx stays untouched.

steps.say: On a Mac, the checker is Review, Check Accessibility. For alt text, Control-click the picture and choose Edit Alt Text. Save a template with File, Save as Template, and find it under File, New from Template.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Review > Check Accessibility
• Alt text: Control-click picture > Edit Alt Text
• File > Save as Template… (.xltx)
• File > New from Template… (⌘ + ⇧ + P)

steps.say: To recap: run the Accessibility Checker before you share. Give pictures alt text, centre across selection instead of merging, and keep text dark. Save reusable forms as templates.

acts.t:
Recap

• Review > Check Accessibility before sharing
• Alt text · no merged cells · strong contrast
• Save as Template; start new files from it

steps.say: Your challenge: the checker may still suggest renaming the sheet and turning the item rows into a table. Do both until it reports no issues. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Get the checker to 'No accessibility issues found'.
Hint: sheet name and the item rows.

Answer: sheet S15-06 Done, cell H10
